sessions.title: Higher derivatives are successive local information
sessions.focus: Extend M10's first derivative into higher derivatives without yet introducing Taylor polynomials.
sessions.purpose: Give higher-order local data a meaning and notation before factorial coefficients appear.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and audit repeated derivatives, their values and their domains for elementary one-variable functions.
sessions.principalObstacle: Repeated differentiation is often treated as symbol pushing; signs, domains and the meaning of each derivative can drift unnoticed.
entryPrerequisites: M02/M03 factorial familiarity from finite counting
requiredOwnership: Compute successive higher derivatives of an elementary one-variable function and evaluate them at a point.
Use f^(n) notation and distinguish derivative order from exponentiation.
Audit signs and domains under repeated differentiation rather than silently enlarging the original function domain.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary one-variable functions already differentiable by M10 rules; no Taylor formula yet.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from polynomial calculation to diagnosis of a repeated-derivative/domain report for log.
sessions.exitCondition: Compute higher derivatives correctly and reject a repeated-derivative report that has both a sign and domain error.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M10 used one derivative to describe first-order local change. If the derivative itself changes, its derivative records that change; differentiating again records the next layer. Taylor approximation will use this whole stack, so signs and domains must remain trustworthy.

Define. Set f^(0)=f, f^(1)=f', f^(2)=f'', and in general f^(n)=(f^(n-1))' wherever that derivative exists. The superscript in parentheses is an order label, not a power: f^(3) is not f cubed. Factorials k!=k(k-1)...1 will later appear because differentiating (x-a)^k exactly k times produces k!.

Connect. M10 already made f' a new function with its own domain. The same rule repeats: a formula for f^(n) is only legal where every differentiation step and the original function are legal.

Explain. Polynomial derivatives eventually vanish. Sine and cosine cycle. e^x repeats itself. Logarithms keep the original x>0 domain even though rational-looking derivative formulas such as 1/x are algebraically defined elsewhere.

Worked example. For q(x)=x^4-2x^2+x, q'=4x^3-4x+1, q''=12x^2-4, q'''=24x and q^(4)=24. At x=1 the successive values are 1,1,8,24,24 for orders 0 through 4. The second derivative is information about how the first derivative changes; it is not a second power of q.

Guided practice. Differentiate sin x four times. Check: cos x, -sin x, -cos x, sin x. The cycle returns after four derivatives.

Distinction check. A derivative formula can look algebraically meaningful outside the original domain without becoming a derivative there.

sessions.title: The unique polynomial that matches derivative data
sessions.focus: Derive Taylor coefficients about an arbitrary center from derivative-matching conditions.
sessions.purpose: Make the Taylor polynomial a forced local object rather than a memorized formula.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct and justify the unique degree-at-most-n centered polynomial whose derivatives through order n match supplied local derivative data.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners may memorize coefficients without understanding why k! appears or may confuse a polynomial coefficient with the corresponding derivative value.
requiredOwnership: Construct a centered Taylor polynomial from derivative data at an arbitrary nonzero center.
Derive the coefficient factor 1/k! from differentiating (x-a)^k exactly k times.
Explain uniqueness among degree-at-most-n polynomials with the same derivative data.
sessions.applicationScope: Finite one-variable polynomials about arbitrary real centers.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from constructing a polynomial to recovering derivative data from centered coefficients and defending uniqueness.
sessions.exitCondition: Build the polynomial from data and reverse the map from coefficients back to derivatives without the coefficient/derivative confusion.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Suppose we know the value, slope, curvature and further derivatives of a function at one point. Which polynomial stores exactly that local data?

Define. Write h=x-a and consider Q(x)=c_0+c_1h+c_2h^2+...+c_nh^n. At x=a, h=0. Q(a)=c_0. Differentiating once and evaluating at a leaves c_1. Differentiating k times makes the h^k term contribute k! c_k while higher powers still contain a factor h and vanish at a.

Explain. To force Q^(k)(a)=f^(k)(a), we must choose c_k=f^(k)(a)/k!. Therefore P_n(x)=sum_{k=0}^n f^(k)(a)(x-a)^k/k!. The factorial is not decoration; it cancels the k! generated by k differentiations.

Uniqueness. If two degree-at-most-n polynomials have the same derivatives through order n at a, their difference D has D(a)=D'(a)=...=D^(n)(a)=0. In centered powers each derivative condition kills one coefficient, so all coefficients of D are zero. The two polynomials are identical.

Worked example. At a=3 suppose f(3)=2, f'(3)=4 and f''(3)=-6. The matching quadratic is 2+4(x-3)-3(x-3)^2. Its second derivative is -6, not -3: -3 is the quadratic coefficient.

Guided practice. At a=-2, data f=1, f'=0, f''=8 give P_2(x)=1+4(x+2)^2.

Distinction check. The term (x-a)^k vanishes at the center for k>0, but its kth derivative does not; this is precisely why higher derivative data can live in the polynomial.

sessions.title: Center, graph and coefficient meaning
sessions.focus: Connect centered polynomial coefficients to value, slope and curvature and make arbitrary-center reasoning habitual.
sessions.purpose: Prevent Maclaurin-only pattern matching and turn algebraic coefficients into local geometric information.
sessions.centralCapability: Translate among graph/local derivative information and centered Taylor coefficients, including recentering a polynomial.
sessions.principalObstacle: At x=a every positive-power term evaluates to zero, tempting the false conclusion that its coefficient or corresponding derivative is zero.
requiredOwnership: Translate value, slope and second-derivative information at a nonzero center into a quadratic local polynomial.
Distinguish the coefficient of (x-a)^2 from the second derivative value.
Recenter an exact polynomial about a new center without treating center 0 as privileged.
sessions.applicationScope: Quadratic local representation and exact recentering of low-degree polynomials.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from graphical derivative information to exact recentering of a supplied polynomial.
sessions.exitCondition: Build a quadratic from graph-derived data and exactly recenter a polynomial around a different point.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A Taylor polynomial is centered information. Changing the center changes its coefficients even when the underlying function is the same.

Connect representations. For P_2(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+f''(a)(x-a)^2/2, the constant term is the graph height at a, the linear coefficient is the tangent slope, and twice the quadratic coefficient is the second derivative. Positive second derivative means local upward curvature; negative means downward curvature.

Why the center matters. At x=a the factors (x-a) and (x-a)^2 are zero, so P_2(a)=f(a). That does not make f'(a) or f''(a) zero. Those derivatives are recovered by differentiating before evaluating.

Worked example. A graph at a=2 has value -1, slope 3 and second derivative 4. Its matching quadratic is -1+3(x-2)+2(x-2)^2. The quadratic coefficient is 2 while the second derivative is 4.

Recenter exact polynomials. If p(x)=x^2, then about a=3 write x=3+h: p=9+6h+h^2. This is not an approximation; because p has degree 2, the degree-2 Taylor polynomial equals p exactly everywhere.

Guided practice. At a=-1, height 5, horizontal tangent and second derivative -2 give 5-(x+1)^2.

Distinction check. Maclaurin means only the special center a=0. It is not another theorem and is not the definition of Taylor approximation.

sessions.title: Derivative matching is local, not a global error guarantee
sessions.focus: Introduce the residual and fixed-degree local order question before Taylor's theorem.
sessions.purpose: Create the need for an error theorem without pretending derivative matching itself supplies one.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute and interpret residuals in explicit examples, separating fixed-degree x→a behavior from global closeness.
sessions.principalObstacle: A polynomial can share several derivatives at a center yet be very inaccurate farther away; a local condition is easily overgeneralized.
requiredOwnership: Compute an explicit residual f-P_n and analyze a scaled residual limit in a case where the algebra is known exactly.
Distinguish fixed-degree local behavior as x approaches the center from an n→infinity series question.
Refute a global-accuracy claim using a concrete far-from-center error despite correct derivative matching.
sessions.applicationScope: Explicit finite functions where residual algebra is directly available; no general Taylor error theorem yet.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from symbolic residual analysis to numerical local-versus-far comparison refuting a global claim.
sessions.exitCondition: Use exact residual data to explain why local derivative matching needs a separate theorem before finite error can be certified.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S02 told us which polynomial matches derivatives. It did not say how close that polynomial is anywhere except in the derivative data at the center.

Define. For a chosen finite polynomial P_n, call R_n(x)=f(x)-P_n(x) the residual or actual approximation error. At this stage R_n is just a difference; no general bound has been proved.

Fixed degree, moving x. If an explicit example gives R_2(a+h)=5h^3, then R_2/h^2=5h→0 as h→0. That says the error is negligible compared with h^2 near the center. It says nothing by itself about h=2.

Different question. Keeping x fixed and letting n grow asks whether a sequence of polynomials converges. That is an infinite-series question and arrives later. Do not merge it with x→a at fixed n.

Worked example. Let f(a+h)=4-h+2h^2-3h^3 and P_2=4-h+2h^2. Then R_2=-3h^3 and R_2/h^2=-3h→0. At h=1, however, the actual error is -3, which may be large for the application.

Guided practice. If R_1(h)=8h^2, then R_1/h=8h→0 near 0; at h=0.5 the error is 2. Local scaling and finite numerical size are different claims.

Distinction check. The general theorem that will control R_n has not been earned yet.

sessions.title: Rolle and MVT: the bounded support bridge for Taylor error
sessions.focus: Supply only the interval theorem machinery needed to prove the Taylor remainder.
sessions.purpose: Close a formal prerequisite gap without turning M12 into a general Mean Value Theorem applications unit.
sessions.centralCapability: Prove/use the compact Rolle→MVT bridge with hypotheses visible and reject illegal applications.
sessions.principalObstacle: A familiar theorem is often invoked from endpoint data alone while continuity or interior differentiability is missing.
entryPrerequisites: M10 derivative definition and local extrema intuition
requiredOwnership: Derive the one-variable Mean Value Theorem from Rolle's theorem using the secant-line subtraction.
State/check continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval before invoking Rolle/MVT.
Reject a Rolle/MVT conclusion when an interior nondifferentiable point destroys the theorem hypothesis.
sessions.applicationScope: Bounded real intervals only; support for Taylor proof.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from theorem reconstruction to a nondifferentiable absolute-value counterexample.
outOfScope: global error estimates other than later Taylor use
sessions.exitCondition: Can reconstruct MVT and identify an exact hypothesis failure in a tempting counterexample.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Taylor's remainder proof needs a way to turn endpoint equalities into a derivative equality somewhere in between. M10 did not own a broad MVT unit, so we make the needed bridge explicit.

Fermat support. If a differentiable function has a local maximum or minimum at an interior point c, then its derivative at c is 0. The derivative quotient from the right and left cannot both have the same nonzero sign at an extremum.

Rolle. If g is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and g(a)=g(b), the EVT gives a maximum and minimum. If g is constant, every interior derivative is 0. Otherwise one extremum occurs inside, and Fermat gives g'(c)=0.

MVT. For f continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), subtract the secant line L(t)=f(a)+m(t-a), where m=[f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a). Then h=f-L has equal endpoint values, so Rolle gives h'(c)=0 and therefore f'(c)=m.

Worked example. For f(t)=t^2 on [1,3], the secant slope is (9-1)/2=4. MVT predicts c in (1,3) with 2c=4, so c=2.

Guided practice. For f(t)=1/t on [1,2], identify the hypotheses and the secant slope -1/2; solving -1/c^2=-1/2 gives c=sqrt(2), which lies inside.

Distinction check. A conclusion that happens to be true does not legalize a theorem invocation whose hypotheses are absent.

sessions.title: Taylor's theorem: derivative matching plus a legal remainder
sessions.focus: Turn a derivative-matching polynomial into a theorem-level local approximation with the Lagrange remainder and all interval/derivative hypotheses visible.
sessions.purpose: Prevent Taylor polynomials from becoming unexplained formulas by showing exactly what theorem connects them to the target function and where the unknown remainder point comes from.
sessions.centralCapability: Reconstruct and audit the one-variable Lagrange-remainder theorem on a bounded interval, including its hypotheses and the role of the intermediate point.
sessions.principalObstacle: The coefficient derivatives are evaluated at the center, which tempts a learner to put the remainder derivative there too.
requiredOwnership: Reconstruct a valid degree-2 Lagrange-remainder proof from derivative matching and Rolle/MVT.
Distinguish the Taylor center from the unknown intermediate remainder point and locate that point between center and evaluation point.
Audit a proposed Taylor-theorem use for the required higher-derivative hypothesis on the whole intervening open interval.
sessions.applicationScope: One-variable finite-order Taylor theorem; representative n=2 proof.
sessions.transferScope: Hypothesis forensics on a piecewise-smooth function crossing an interior point where the next derivative fails.
sessions.exitCondition: Prove the n=2 remainder and reject an illegal application despite a valid Taylor polynomial at the center.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. A polynomial can match f and its derivatives at a center and still separate from f away from that center. We need a theorem that turns derivative matching into a statement about the residual.

Define. For center a, let P_n be the degree-n Taylor polynomial and R_n(x)=f(x)-P_n(x). If f has n continuous derivatives on the closed interval joining a and x and f^(n+1) exists at every interior point, then for some c strictly between a and x,
R_n(x)=f^(n+1)(c)(x-a)^(n+1)/(n+1)!.
The point c is supplied by the theorem; it is not automatically a or x.

Connect. S02 forced P_n^(k)(a)=f^(k)(a) for k≤n. S05 supplied Rolle/MVT. Those two facts are exactly the ingredients used in the remainder proof.

Explain the proof architecture on degree 1, not on the fixed Main instance. Fix a≠x and choose M so
f(x)-P_1(x)=M(x-a)^2.
Set g(t)=f(t)-P_1(t)-M(t-a)^2. Then g(x)=0, while derivative matching at a gives g(a)=g'(a)=0. Rolle applied to g between a and x gives an interior point d with g'(d)=0. Applying Rolle to g' between a and d gives c strictly between a and x with g''(c)=0. Since g''(t)=f''(t)-2M, we obtain M=f''(c)/2 and hence
f(x)-P_1(x)=f''(c)(x-a)^2/2.
The general theorem repeats the same zero-forcing idea enough times; Main asks you to reconstruct the next degree rather than copy this proof verbatim.

Worked example. Let f(t)=ln t, center a=1 and evaluate x=1.2. For n=1, P_1(t)=t-1 because f(1)=0 and f'(1)=1. Since ln has the required derivatives on [1,1.2], Taylor's theorem gives
ln(1.2)-0.2=f''(c)(0.2)^2/2
for some c∈(1,1.2). Since f''(c)=-1/c^2, the remainder is negative. We have not yet replaced c by a numerical bound; S07 will do that.

Guided practice. For f(t)=e^t, center 0 and a first-degree polynomial evaluated at x=0.3, write only the legal Lagrange-remainder statement and locate c. Check: e^0.3-(1+0.3)=e^c(0.3)^2/2 for some c∈(0,0.3). Do not set c=0 merely because the polynomial coefficients use derivatives at 0.

Distinction check. "P_n uses derivatives at a" and "the remainder contains f^(n+1)(c)" are different theorem roles. Existence of the Taylor polynomial at one point is not enough to invoke the Lagrange theorem across an interval where the next derivative fails.

sessions.title: From remainder formula to certified tolerance
sessions.focus: Turn the unknown Lagrange point into a defensible error bound and use that bound to choose approximation order or center.
sessions.purpose: Make truncation an accountable tolerance decision rather than “drop small terms.”
sessions.centralCapability: Bound the relevant next derivative on the whole interval and convert Taylor's remainder into a certified numerical error inequality.
sessions.principalObstacle: Using the derivative value at the center or endpoint as though it were automatically the maximum can understate error.
requiredOwnership: Find or justify a uniform bound M for the relevant next derivative on the entire interval between center and target.
Compute a certified Lagrange error bound and distinguish it from the actual error.
Choose among candidate degrees using a stated tolerance rather than visual stability or the first omitted term.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary exp/log/trig examples with simple derivative bounds.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from degree selection for sin to interval-bound construction for log.
sessions.exitCondition: Can reject an endpoint-only derivative bound and produce a legal interval-wide certificate.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S06 says the remainder uses f^(n+1)(c), but c is unknown. To make the theorem operational we bound that derivative everywhere c could be.

If |f^(n+1)(t)|≤M for every t between a and x, then |R_n(x)|≤M|x-a|^(n+1)/(n+1)!. M must cover the whole intervening interval. A value at one endpoint is a bound only if you justify why no larger magnitude occurs elsewhere.

Worked example. Approximate e^0.25 by P_2=1+0.25+0.25^2/2. On [0,0.25], e^t≤e^0.25<1.3, so |R_2|<1.3(0.25)^3/6≈0.00339. This is an upper bound; it is not an assertion that the actual error equals 0.00339.

Degree choice. A tolerance is a public inequality to satisfy. Test candidate degrees by their proved bounds; do not stop because successive decimal answers look similar.

Guided practice. For cos(0.2), the degree-2 Maclaurin polynomial has fourth? Careful: the Lagrange remainder for degree 2 uses the third derivative sin, so the simple M=1 bound is |R_2|≤0.2^3/6. State the theorem you are actually using rather than jumping to the next nonzero series term.

Distinction check. “First omitted nonzero term” can be a useful heuristic in special series, but Lagrange certification comes from a theorem and an interval-wide derivative bound.

sessions.title: Big-O and little-o are precise error statements
sessions.focus: Compress local error information into bounded-ratio and vanishing-ratio notation without turning the symbols into vague approximation signs.
sessions.purpose: Give the canonical module title's 'asymptotics' component a precise deterministic foundation tied to M09 limits and M12 remainder bounds.
sessions.centralCapability: Prove and distinguish local O and o statements from inequalities/limits.
sessions.principalObstacle: O and o are often read as interchangeable versions of 'small,' hiding constants, neighborhoods and limit strength.
requiredOwnership: Prove an O statement by exhibiting bounded ratio or an explicit constant/neighborhood.
Prove an o statement by a ratio limit and distinguish it from O of the same scale.
Translate a Taylor-style bound of order h^(n+1) into both O(h^(n+1)) and the weaker-scale o(h^n) consequence.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from explicit polynomial residual to reasoning from an inequality certificate and constructing a counterexample to an overstrong o claim.
sessions.exitCondition: Can prove true O/o statements and reject an unjustified little-o upgrade.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. Repeating “there exists a constant and a small enough neighborhood” is cumbersome. Order notation compresses that logic, but only if its definition remains visible.

As h→0, r(h)=O(h^k) means |r(h)/h^k| stays bounded on some punctured neighborhood; equivalently there are C,δ>0 with |r(h)|≤C|h|^k whenever 0<|h|<δ. By contrast r(h)=o(h^k) means r(h)/h^k→0.

Example. r(h)=3h^2+h^3 has r/h^2=3+h, bounded but not tending to 0. So r=O(h^2) but not o(h^2). Yet r/h=3h+h^2→0, so r=o(h).

Taylor link. If S07 gives |R_n(a+h)|≤C|h|^(n+1) locally, then R_n=O(h^(n+1)). Dividing by |h|^n leaves at most C|h|→0, hence R_n=o(h^n). The second statement is weaker in scale, not a synonym.

Worked example. If |E(h)|≤7|h|^3 for |h|<0.1, then E=O(h^3) and E=o(h^2). We cannot conclude E=o(h^3); E=7h^3 satisfies the same bound but has ratio 7.

Guided practice. h^4 is o(h^3) and O(h^4); h^3 is O(h^3) but not o(h^3).

Distinction check. Neither O nor o is an informal equals sign. Always say what variable approaches what limit.

sessions.title: Asymptotic equivalence and leading scale
sessions.focus: Define f~g by a ratio-one limit and separate relative equivalence from absolute closeness.
sessions.purpose: Complete the bounded deterministic asymptotic vocabulary needed later without importing probabilistic or full asymptotic-series machinery.
sessions.centralCapability: Prove and interpret asymptotic equivalence at finite or infinite limiting points.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners often replace ratio-one equivalence by the weaker/different condition f-g→0.
requiredOwnership: Prove f~g from the ratio limit or from f=g+o(g) where g is eventually nonzero.
Distinguish asymptotic equivalence from the condition f-g→0 using counterexamples.
Apply the same definition to deterministic sequences as n→infinity and interpret relative rather than absolute error.
sessions.transferScope: Change limiting variable from h→0 to n→∞ and make the absolute difference diverge while relative error vanishes.
sessions.exitCondition: Can defend ratio-one equivalence even when absolute difference grows, and reject difference-zero as a definition.
sessions.lesson:
Define. As x→c, f(x)~g(x) means f(x)/g(x)→1 wherever g is nonzero sufficiently near the limit point. Equivalently, f=g+o(g) when that statement is well-defined.

Relative, not absolute. If f=2h+5h^2 and g=2h, then f/g=1+(5/2)h→1. The second term is negligible relative to the first.

A trap. f-g→0 does not imply f~g. For f(h)=h and g(h)=2h, the difference -h→0 while f/g=1/2. Conversely, f~g does not require the absolute difference to vanish at infinity.

Worked example. As n→∞, n+1~n because (n+1)/n→1 even though the difference stays 1.

Guided practice. n+sqrt(n)~n because the relative correction is 1/sqrt(n)→0; its absolute correction grows without bound.

Taylor connection. A local relation f(a+h)=A h^k+o(h^k), A≠0, implies f(a+h)~A h^k. This identifies the leading scale, not a finite numerical tolerance.

Distinction check. The informal symbol ≈ has no fixed limit-theorem meaning here; ~ does.

sessions.title: Infinite series are limits of finite partial sums
sessions.focus: Close the hidden prerequisite gap between M09 sequence limits and Taylor series.
sessions.purpose: Make infinity a limit operation rather than an algebraic ellipsis.
sessions.centralCapability: Define and analyze an infinite series through its partial-sum sequence, deriving the geometric-series result from M09.
sessions.principalObstacle: Writing infinitely many terms can tempt algebraic manipulations that are valid only after convergence is established.
requiredOwnership: Define convergence of an infinite series via the sequence of finite partial sums.
Derive the geometric-series sum for |r|<1 from the finite sum formula and q^N→0.
Reject algebra on a divergent series by inspecting its partial sums.
sessions.applicationScope: Geometric and simple partial-sum examples only.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from convergent geometric derivation to auditing a famous divergent alternating manipulation.
sessions.exitCondition: Never assigns an ordinary sum to a series before its partial sums converge.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. The symbol ... is not a permission to perform infinitely many arithmetic operations at once. M09 already knows how sequences converge, so we define an infinite sum through a sequence of finite sums.

For numbers a_0,a_1,... define S_N=sum_{n=0}^N a_n. The infinite series sum a_n converges to S exactly when the sequence S_N converges to S.

Geometric bridge. For r≠1,
1+r+...+r^N=(1-r^(N+1))/(1-r).
If |r|<1, M09 gives r^(N+1)→0, so the series sums to 1/(1-r). If |r|>1 or r=1, the partial sums do not converge; for r=-1 they oscillate.

Worked example. sum_{n=0}∞ (1/3)^n has S_N=[1-(1/3)^(N+1)]/(1-1/3)→3/2.

Guided practice. sum 2(1/5)^n converges to 2/(1-1/5)=5/2.

Distinction check. Manipulations such as S=1-1+1-... and S=1-S presuppose an ordinary convergent sum. The partial sums decide whether that premise exists.

sessions.title: Power series have a center and a convergence region
sessions.focus: Introduce power series as x-dependent series and use geometric examples to make center and region concrete.
sessions.purpose: Supply only the power-series language Taylor series needs, without opening a general series-test course.
sessions.centralCapability: Analyze geometric power series about arbitrary centers, including convergence region, sum and partial-sum meaning.
sessions.principalObstacle: The summation index or standard powers x^n can distract from the actual center encoded by (x-a)^n.
requiredOwnership: Identify the center of a power series and express its geometric ratio in terms of x-a.
Determine a directly justified convergence region and sum for a geometric power series.
Diagnose a false center claim and endpoint divergence without invoking unowned general convergence tests.
sessions.applicationScope: Geometric power series where convergence follows directly from |r|<1.
sessions.transferScope: Changed to center diagnosis and endpoint behavior for a differently shifted series.
sessions.exitCondition: Reads center from the powers and proves the region from the geometric ratio.
sessions.lesson:
Define. A power series about a is sum_{n=0}∞ c_n(x-a)^n. For each fixed x it becomes an ordinary numerical series; convergence is therefore a question about its partial sums at that x.

Geometric anchor. sum ((x-a)/R)^n is geometric with ratio r=(x-a)/R. It converges exactly when |x-a|<|R| and then sums to 1/[1-(x-a)/R].

Center. The point a is where every positive-power term vanishes. It need not be 0. The lower summation index n=0 says where indexing starts, not where the series is centered.

Worked example. sum ((x+2)/4)^n is centered at -2 and converges when |x+2|<4, i.e. -6<x<2. Its sum there is 1/[1-(x+2)/4].

Representation. Partial-sum graphs are finite polynomials. At points where the series converges they may approach a limiting function; outside the convergence region higher partial sums can move farther away.

Guided practice. sum ((x-5)/2)^n is centered at 5 and converges for 3<x<7.

Boundary. We are not proving the full theorem that arbitrary power series have a radius of convergence, nor learning a battery of tests.

sessions.title: A Taylor series is a candidate, not a promise
sessions.focus: Continue the finite derivative-matching pattern indefinitely while keeping partial sums, series convergence and target equality distinct.
sessions.purpose: Prevent coefficient generation from being mistaken for a representation theorem.
sessions.centralCapability: Construct a Taylor-series candidate and state exactly what remains unproved before identifying it with the function.
sessions.principalObstacle: The familiar equals sign f(x)=sum... is often written before convergence or equality has been established.
requiredOwnership: Construct the Taylor-series candidate about an arbitrary center from all derivative data.
Identify the nth Taylor polynomial as the nth finite partial sum of that candidate.
Refuse to infer unobserved higher coefficients or equality with the target from finitely many Taylor polynomials.
sessions.applicationScope: Formal candidate construction; equality postponed to S14.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from complete derivative pattern to finite observed partial polynomials where extrapolating an infinite pattern is underdetermined.
sessions.exitCondition: Uses 'candidate' language until convergence-to-function is justified.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S02 built P_n for any finite n. If derivatives of every order exist, we can write the infinite coefficient pattern
sum_{k=0}∞ f^(k)(a)(x-a)^k/k!.
This is the Taylor-series candidate about a.

Finite versus infinite. Its nth partial sum is exactly P_n. That identity is algebraic. It does not prove the sequence P_n(x) converges as n→∞, and even convergence to some number would not yet prove the limit is f(x).

Three questions must remain separate:
1. Do all required derivatives at a exist?
2. Does the resulting numerical series converge at the chosen x?
3. If it converges, is its sum f(x)?

Worked example. If f^(k)(1)=2 for every k, the candidate is 2 sum (x-1)^k/k!. Writing this candidate is legal from the data; claiming it equals f needs additional information.

Finite-pattern warning. Seeing P_0,P_1,P_2,P_3 does not determine P_4 or later coefficients unless a rule for higher derivatives is supplied. M02 already taught that finite prefixes do not prove all-future behavior.

Guided practice. If all derivatives at a are zero, the Taylor-series candidate is the zero series. Whether the function itself is zero nearby is a different question reserved for S17.

sessions.title: Canonical elementary candidates by derivative pattern
sessions.focus: Generate exp/sin/cos Taylor candidates and transform them through simple scaling or recentering.
sessions.purpose: Build reusable canonical expansions from derivative structure instead of memorized lists.
sessions.centralCapability: Generate representative Taylor polynomials/series candidates from derivative cycles at the correct center.
sessions.principalObstacle: Memorized Maclaurin formulas are easily mis-scaled or reused at the wrong center.
requiredOwnership: Generate the exponential, sine or cosine Taylor coefficients from their derivative patterns rather than quote an unexplained formula.
Handle affine input scaling correctly in a canonical Maclaurin candidate.
Construct a canonical candidate about a nonzero center.
sessions.applicationScope: e^x, sin, cos and affine versions; equality proof remains S14.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from scaled Maclaurin cosine to exponential recentered at 1.
outOfScope: termwise series operations as a theorem
sessions.exitCondition: Can reconstruct canonical candidates when coefficients are not handed over.
sessions.lesson:
For e^x, every derivative is e^x, so at a=0 every derivative value is 1 and the candidate is sum x^k/k!. For sin x, derivatives cycle sin,cos,-sin,-cos; at 0 only odd terms remain with alternating signs. Cos has the even alternating pattern.

Generate, do not chant. For cos(3x), repeated chain-rule scaling gives factors 3^k; equivalently substitute the centered variable into the derivative pattern only after checking the scaling. This yields 1-(3x)^2/2!+(3x)^4/4!-....

Nonzero center. For e^x about a, every derivative at a is e^a, so the candidate is e^a sum (x-a)^k/k!. This is a centered construction, not a translated slogan.

Worked example. sin(2x) has P_5=2x-(2x)^3/3!+(2x)^5/5!.

Guided practice. cos x about a=pi has derivative data -1,0,1,0,-1,... and begins -1+(x-pi)^2/2!-(x-pi)^4/4!+....

Boundary. We are still constructing candidates. S14 earns equality with the target.

sessions.title: When the Taylor series actually equals the function
sessions.focus: Use remainder-to-zero as the decisive bridge from finite Taylor polynomials to a valid infinite representation.
sessions.purpose: Separate convergence of a numerical series from proof that its sum is the original function.
sessions.centralCapability: Prove selected canonical Taylor representations by driving the finite Taylor remainder to zero.
sessions.principalObstacle: A convergent derivative-generated series can be mistaken for the target function without controlling f-P_n.
requiredOwnership: Use the identity f=P_n+R_n and a proved R_n(x)→0 to justify equality between a Taylor series and f at a fixed x.
Prove the factorial tail |x|^n/n! tends to zero for fixed x using an eventual geometric bound.
Reject the inference 'the Taylor series converges, therefore it equals f' and repair it with a remainder argument.
sessions.applicationScope: e^x, sin x, cos x for fixed real x.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from direct e^x representation proof to logic audit and repair for sine.
sessions.exitCondition: Never turns a convergent candidate into f without a target-equality argument.
sessions.lesson:
The finite identity is always f(x)=P_n(x)+R_n(x) whenever P_n and R_n are defined. Therefore if, for a fixed x, R_n(x)→0 as n→∞, the partial sums P_n(x) converge to f(x). This is the bridge.

Factorial tail. For fixed A=|x|, let u_n=A^n/n!. Once n+1≥2A, u_{n+1}/u_n=A/(n+1)≤1/2. The tail is then dominated by a decaying geometric sequence, so u_n→0.

For e^x about 0, Taylor's theorem gives |R_n(x)|≤e^|x| |x|^(n+1)/(n+1)! for fixed x. The constant e^|x| does not affect the limit; factorial tail wins, so R_n→0 and the candidate equals e^x for every real x.

For sin/cos, every derivative has magnitude at most 1, so the same style of bound is even simpler.

Worked example. For cos x, |R_n(x)|≤|x|^(n+1)/(n+1)! for any fixed x when using the degree-n polynomial. Hence the full cosine candidate represents cos x on all real inputs.

Guided practice. Explain why 'the coefficients look right' is insufficient until the remainder bridge is supplied.

Distinction check. Series convergence answers “does P_n(x) approach some value?” Remainder decay answers “is that value f(x)?”

sessions.title: Generate the local model when nobody says 'use Taylor'
sessions.focus: Transfer from formulas to graph, derivative-table and contextual local information.
sessions.purpose: Directly address the documented gap between recognizing/applying a supplied expansion and generating one in a novel context.
sessions.centralCapability: Choose the centered variable and construct a finite local polynomial from contextual or graphical derivative data without a Taylor template.
sessions.principalObstacle: Topic cues can carry procedural performance; removing the cue exposes whether the learner recognizes what local data mean.
requiredOwnership: Generate a quadratic local model from contextual derivative data without a supplied Taylor formula.
Interpret the linear and quadratic contributions in terms of local change/curvature rather than coefficient recital.
State what additional next-derivative information is needed before a certified finite error bound is available.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from numeric context table to graphical local features at a negative center.
sessions.exitCondition: Recognizes and constructs the local polynomial when the word Taylor is absent.
sessions.lesson:
Research evidence on advanced students shows an important split: many can interpret a supplied Taylor expression yet struggle to generate the right expansion in a new physical setting. This session removes the chapter cue.

Strategy. Identify the center a from the operating point. Introduce h=x-a. Translate local data: value→constant term, first derivative→linear coefficient, second derivative/2→quadratic coefficient. Only then calculate.

Worked context. A calibration response C(p) at p=10 has C=50, C'=2 units/parameter and C''=-0.6 units/parameter^2. The matching quadratic is 50+2h-0.3h^2. At h=0.1 the linear contribution is +0.2 and quadratic correction -0.003.

What it does not know. Without a bound on C''' over the interval, this quadratic does not come with a certified Lagrange error. Local model construction and error certification are separate capabilities.

Graph representation. Height, tangent slope and concavity at a center encode the same derivative data. A graph can suggest signs and relative shape but does not invent numerical derivative magnitudes that are not supplied.

Guided practice. Given value 4, slope -1 and second derivative 6 at a=-2, build 4-(x+2)+3(x+2)^2.

Distinction check. “Use Taylor” is not a capability. Recognizing local derivative data and creating the representation is.

sessions.title: Higher degree is not globally safer: center and convergence region
sessions.focus: Use a geometric-function example to show Taylor partial sums can worsen outside their convergence region and that recentering can matter more than adding terms.
sessions.purpose: Destroy the global-monotone-improvement misconception and make center choice operational.
sessions.centralCapability: Diagnose a failed far-field Taylor expansion and construct a better legal recentering when the function permits it.
sessions.principalObstacle: Success near a center encourages the false rule that more terms improve approximation everywhere.
requiredOwnership: Demonstrate with exact partial sums that increasing Taylor degree can worsen approximation outside a convergence region.
Explain the failure through the geometric ratio/center rather than blaming arithmetic.
Recenter a geometric-function expansion and compare relative ratios at a target point.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from failure diagnosis at x=-2 to constructing a new center near x=0.9 and comparing convergence ratios.
sessions.exitCondition: Knows when adding terms is structurally wrong and can change center instead.
sessions.lesson:
For f(x)=1/(1-x), the Maclaurin Taylor partial sums are P_n=1+x+...+x^n because the function is the geometric sum only for |x|<1.

Inside |x|<1, the omitted geometric tail shrinks. Outside, powers x^n need not shrink at all. More terms can therefore make the finite polynomial farther from f.

Worked example. At x=-1.5, f=0.4 while P_1=-0.5, P_2=1.75, P_3=-1.625; the sequence is not settling because the geometric ratio has magnitude 1.5.

Center choice. Around a=0.5, write h=x-0.5:
1/(1-x)=1/(0.5-h)=2/(1-2h)=2 sum (2h)^n for |h|<0.5.
The same function gets a new local representation and new convergence region.

Guided practice. Compare target x=0.75: ratio from center 0 is 0.75; from center 0.5 it is 0.5, so the recentered geometric tail contracts faster.

Distinction check. Degree and center are different design choices.

sessions.title: Smooth does not mean analytic
sessions.focus: Use a flat smooth function to separate existence of all derivatives from equality with the Taylor series.
sessions.purpose: Close the most dangerous logical gap in the legacy Taylor route.
sessions.centralCapability: Analyze a smooth nonanalytic counterexample and distinguish a convergent Taylor series from a series representing the function.
sessions.principalObstacle: If every derivative at a point exists, it feels as though those infinitely many data must determine the nearby function.
requiredOwnership: Define operationally what it means for a function to be represented by its Taylor series near a center.
Use a flat-function example with all derivatives zero at the center to show smoothness does not imply analyticity.
Distinguish a Taylor series that diverges from one that converges perfectly but to the wrong function.
sessions.transferScope: Changed to adding a linear analytic term to the flat function, producing a nonzero but still incorrect Taylor representation.
sessions.exitCondition: Can name exactly which implication fails in smooth⇒analytic reasoning.
sessions.lesson:
Operational definition. A function is analytic at a when, on some neighborhood of a, its Taylor-series partial sums converge to the function itself. Having derivatives of every order is necessary for writing the Taylor candidate, but not sufficient for representation.

Flat example. Define phi(0)=0 and phi(x)=exp(-1/x^2) for x≠0. A standard induction shows each derivative for x≠0 is a polynomial in 1/x times exp(-1/x^2). As x→0, set y=1/|x|→∞. Exponential decay exp(-y^2) beats every fixed power y^m; using the already-established exponential series, e^(y^2) is eventually at least a sufficiently high polynomial power. Thus every derivative extends to 0 with value 0. So phi is C-infinity and phi^(k)(0)=0 for every k.

Its Taylor-series candidate at 0 is therefore 0+0x+0x^2+...=0. That series converges—to 0. But phi(x)>0 for every x≠0, however close to 0. The failure is not series divergence; it is convergence to the wrong function.

Worked contrast. e^x is smooth and, by S14 remainder decay, analytic everywhere. The extra property is representation, not merely derivative existence.

Guided practice. Adding a flat function to a polynomial preserves the polynomial's Taylor coefficients at 0 while changing the nearby function away from 0.

Distinction check. Infinite derivative data at one point need not determine a general smooth function.

sessions.title: Approximation forensics: choose the strength of claim
sessions.focus: Audit mixed claims about O/o notation, error bounds, Taylor-series convergence and representation.
sessions.purpose: Make theorem legality and claim strength an explicit capability before final synthesis.
sessions.centralCapability: Classify approximation statements by what evidence actually supports them and repair overclaims.
sessions.principalObstacle: Correct-looking formulas can hide an unjustified upgrade from bound to equality, O to o, or convergence to representation.
requiredOwnership: Distinguish consequences that follow from an explicit remainder bound from stronger little-o claims that need extra evidence.
Separate Taylor-series convergence from equality to the target via the remainder criterion.
Audit an O statement for its hidden constant/neighborhood before using it as a finite numerical error certificate.
sessions.transferScope: Changed from logical truth-table audit to a numerical misuse of a local O statement.
sessions.exitCondition: Chooses only conclusions actually licensed by the supplied evidence.
sessions.lesson:
Forensics asks: what is the public evidence, and what claim strength does it license?

If |R(h)|≤5|h|^3 near 0, then R=O(h^3) and R=o(h^2). It does not imply R=o(h^3); R=5h^3 is a counterexample.

If a Taylor series converges at x, that alone does not identify its sum with f(x). The finite identity f=P_n+R_n plus R_n→0 does.

If f(a+h)=P(h)+O(h^2), the O symbol hides some constant C and some sufficiently small neighborhood. It does not by itself say C=1, and it does not say a specific h such as 0.5 lies inside that neighborhood.

Worked audit. A report changes O(h^3) to “error exactly h^3.” Reject: O is a bound class, not an equality or coefficient.

Guided practice. A report changes R_n→0 at one fixed x to uniform accuracy on an interval. Reject: pointwise remainder decay at one x does not establish a uniform statement.

Boundary. This session adds no theorem. It disciplines use of existing ones.

sessions.title: Synthesis: build, certify, state only what is true
sessions.focus: Coordinate center, degree, finite error, asymptotic notation and infinite representation without being told which chapter tool to use.
sessions.purpose: Make M12 exit competence an organized argument rather than isolated formula recall.
sessions.centralCapability: Choose and defend a finite Taylor model, certify its error, express its local order honestly and separate any infinite-series representation claim.
sessions.principalObstacle: A synthesis problem exposes whether the learner can choose the right strength of claim without a procedural label.
requiredOwnership: Choose between candidate Taylor degrees by a certified tolerance and compute the selected approximation.
Translate the selected finite error structure into an honest local O statement with the limiting variable stated.
Justify an infinite Taylor representation only through the established remainder-to-zero criterion.
Transfer the same workflow to a nonzero center with a different function and error order.
sessions.applicationScope: Elementary exp/trig synthesis with explicit derivative bounds.
sessions.transferScope: Nonzero-center sine local model with a changed tolerance and no need for a full infinite representation.
sessions.exitCondition: Produces a complete bounded argument whose every claim has the right theorem and scope.
sessions.lesson:
Synthesis workflow:
1. Identify the operating center and displacement.
2. Generate the finite derivative-matching polynomial.
3. State the theorem hypotheses required for the remainder.
4. Find an interval-wide derivative bound and test the public tolerance.
5. Compress the local residual with O/o notation only after the bound is known.
6. If an infinite Taylor representation is claimed, separately prove remainder→0 as degree grows.
7. Stop before future machinery.

Worked synthesis. For e^h near 0, compare degrees 1 and 2 under a supplied bound for e^t on the target interval. Choose the first degree whose Lagrange bound meets the tolerance; do not choose by decimal resemblance.

Guided synthesis. For sin(a+h) at a=pi/6, derive the quadratic from value/slope/curvature and use |third derivative|≤1 to obtain a cubic-order error certificate.

Final distinction. A finite model can be excellent without the infinite Taylor series being needed; an infinite representation can be mathematically true without being the best finite approximation for a far-away target.

T22V3::SIDE267::S01-M@1.prompt: For f(x)=x^5-3x^3+2, compute f', f'', and f'''. Evaluate f'(1), f''(1), and f'''(1). State explicitly what f''' means; do not treat the parenthesized 3 as an exponent.

T22V3::SIDE267::S01-T@1.prompt: A report about g(x)=ln x says g'(x)=1/x, g''(x)=-1/x^2, g'''(x)=-2/x^3, and then declares these derivative formulas valid for every x≠0. Audit the report: correct the third derivative and state the legal real domain of g and of these derivatives.

T22V3::SIDE267::S02-M@1.prompt: At the center a=2 a smooth function has f(2)=5, f'(2)=-1, f''(2)=6, and f'''(2)=-12. Construct the unique degree-at-most-3 polynomial whose derivatives through order 3 match these data. Differentiate your polynomial enough to verify all four matching conditions.

T22V3::SIDE267::S02-T@1.prompt: Consider q(x)=4+3(x+1)-2(x+1)^2+5(x+1)^3. Recover q(-1), q'(-1), q''(-1), and q'''(-1) from the centered coefficients. Explain why the quadratic coefficient -2 is not the value q''(-1). Could a different degree-at-most-3 polynomial have all four of the same derivative values at -1? Justify.

T22V3::SIDE267::S03-M@1.prompt: At x=1 a graph of f passes through y=2, has a horizontal tangent, and has second derivative f''(1)=-6. Construct the quadratic Taylor polynomial about a=1. State the quadratic coefficient and the second-derivative value separately, and explain their relationship.

T22V3::SIDE267::S03-T@1.prompt: Recenter the exact polynomial p(x)=x^2-4x+7 about a=3 in powers of (x-3), using value/derivative data at 3. Verify that your centered expression expands back to p(x). Explain why this is exact rather than merely local.

T22V3::SIDE267::S04-M@1.prompt: Write h=x-2. Suppose f(x)=7-h+4h^2+9h^3 and P_2(x)=7-h+4h^2. Compute R_2=f-P_2. Evaluate lim_{h→0} R_2/h^2. Then compute the actual error at h=1 and explain why the limit statement is local rather than a global accuracy guarantee.

T22V3::SIDE267::S04-T@1.prompt: Let g(1+h)=1+h+100h^3, and let L(1+h)=1+h be the degree-1 polynomial matching g's value and slope at h=0. A report says, “Because value and slope match, L is accurate everywhere.” Compute the error at h=0.01 and at h=0.5, analyze (g-L)/h as h→0, and use these facts to audit the report.

T22V3::SIDE267::S05-M@1.prompt: Let f be continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b), with a<b. Prove the Mean Value Theorem by subtracting the secant line and applying Rolle's theorem: show there is c∈(a,b) with f'(c)=[f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a). State where each hypothesis is used.

T22V3::SIDE267::S05-T@1.prompt: A student applies Rolle's theorem to f(x)=|x| on [-1,1] because f(-1)=f(1)=1 and concludes that some c∈(-1,1) has f'(c)=0. Audit the invocation by checking every Rolle hypothesis and the actual derivative behavior on (-1,0), at 0, and on (0,1).

T22V3::SIDE267::S06-M@1.prompt: Let a<x. Suppose f,f',f'' are continuous on [a,x] and f''' exists at every point of (a,x). Let P_2(t)=f(a)+f'(a)(t-a)+f''(a)(t-a)^2/2. Prove that there is some c∈(a,x) such that f(x)-P_2(x)=f'''(c)(x-a)^3/6. You may use the Rolle/MVT bridge already established in this module. Your proof must make clear why c lies between a and x and must not assume c=a.

T22V3::SIDE267::S06-T@1.prompt: Let f(t)=|t|^3, take center a=-1/2 and evaluation point x=1/2, and consider the degree-2 Taylor polynomial at a. A proposed solution says: “The degree-2 Taylor polynomial exists at a, so Taylor's theorem guarantees c∈(-1/2,1/2) with f(x)-P_2(x)=f'''(c)(x-a)^3/6.” Audit this claim. Compute the needed derivatives on t<0 and t>0, identify the theorem hypothesis that fails, and use the actual remainder together with the possible values of f''' where it exists to show concretely that this invocation cannot be correct.

T22V3::SIDE267::S07-M@1.prompt: Approximate sin(0.3) about 0. Compare the degree-1 Taylor polynomial P_1(x)=x with the degree-3 polynomial P_3(x)=x-x^3/6. Using the Lagrange remainder with the defensible bound M=1 for all relevant sine/cosine derivatives, compute an error bound for each at x=0.3. Which of these two degrees can certify absolute error below 0.0004? Give the corresponding approximation.

T22V3::SIDE267::S07-T@1.prompt: Use the degree-2 Taylor polynomial of ln x about a=1 to approximate ln(1.1). Build the polynomial, find a valid bound M for |f'''(t)| on [1,1.1], and give a certified Lagrange error bound. A proposed solution uses |f'''(1.1)| as M without justification; explain why that is not automatically a valid interval bound.

T22V3::SIDE267::S08-M@1.prompt: As h→0 let r(h)=7h^3+h^4. Prove that r(h)=O(h^3) and r(h)=o(h^2). Decide, with a ratio limit, whether r(h)=o(h^3).

T22V3::SIDE267::S08-T@1.prompt: An unknown error E satisfies |E(h)|≤4|h|^4 whenever |h|<0.2. What O and o conclusions can you justify from this certificate as h→0? In particular, justify E=O(h^4) and E=o(h^3), and determine whether the certificate alone forces E=o(h^4). If not, give a concrete E satisfying the certificate that disproves that stronger conclusion.

T22V3::SIDE267::S09-M@1.prompt: As h→0 let f(h)=2h+5h^2 and g(h)=2h. Prove f~g. Then consider p(h)=h and q(h)=2h: show p-q→0 but p is not asymptotic to q. Explain why this disproves the rule “difference tending to zero means asymptotic equivalence.”

T22V3::SIDE267::S09-T@1.prompt: For sequences a_n=n+sqrt(n) and b_n=n, determine whether a_n~b_n as n→∞. Also determine the behavior of a_n-b_n. Explain how both results can be true at once in terms of relative versus absolute error.

T22V3::SIDE267::S10-M@1.prompt: Starting from the finite geometric-sum formula, analyze the infinite series sum_{n=0}^∞ 3(1/4)^n through its partial sums S_N. Derive a formula for S_N and take the limit to obtain the sum.

T22V3::SIDE267::S10-T@1.prompt: A calculation writes S=1-1+1-1+... and then S=1-S, concluding S=1/2. Under the ordinary definition of series convergence used here, audit this argument by writing the partial-sum sequence and deciding whether the series has a sum. Identify the invalid premise in the algebraic manipulation.

T22V3::SIDE267::S11-M@1.prompt: Analyze the power series sum_{n=0}^∞ ((x-2)/3)^n. Identify its center, derive exactly where it converges using the geometric-series criterion, determine its sum there, and check what happens at both boundary points.

T22V3::SIDE267::S11-T@1.prompt: A student sees sum_{n=0}^∞ ((x+1)/2)^n and calls it a Maclaurin series because the index starts at n=0. Audit that claim. Identify the actual center, give the convergence interval from the geometric ratio, and decide convergence at x=1 and x=-3.

T22V3::SIDE267::S12-M@1.prompt: A function has derivatives of every order at a=2 and satisfies f^(k)(2)=(-1)^k k! for every k≥0. Write P_3(x), write the full Taylor-series candidate, and state separately what must still be established before you may claim the series represents f(x) at a particular x≠2.

T22V3::SIDE267::S12-T@1.prompt: Centered at a=-1, someone provides only these finite Taylor polynomials: P_0=2, P_1=2+3h, P_2=2+3h-h^2, P_3=2+3h-h^2+4h^3, where h=x+1.
